questions.prompt: Two-phase locking (2PL) guarantees conflict serializability. What does it NOT guarantee?

options.text: That transactions acquire locks before use

questions.explanation: 2PL enforces a growing phase then a shrinking phase, which guarantees serializability but says nothing about deadlock — two transactions can still wait on each other's locks in a cycle.

questions.prompt: Which variant of 2PL prevents cascading rollbacks by holding all exclusive locks until commit?
questions.explanation: Strict 2PL retains write locks until commit or abort, so no other transaction can read uncommitted data — hence no cascading aborts. Conservative 2PL acquires all locks up front and is deadlock-free but impractical.

questions.prompt: In the wait-die deadlock prevention scheme, when an older transaction requests a lock held by a younger one, the older transaction:
questions.explanation: Wait-die is non-pre-emptive: an older (smaller timestamp) transaction waits, while a younger one requesting an older transaction's lock is aborted. Wound-wait is the pre-emptive mirror image.

questions.prompt: Under basic timestamp ordering, transaction T issues read(X) and TS(T) < W-timestamp(X). What happens?

options.text: The read proceeds and R-timestamp(X) is updated
The read returns the previous version of X
T waits until the writer commits

questions.explanation: T needs a value that has already been overwritten by a younger transaction, so the read is too late and T is rolled back. Option D describes multiversion timestamp ordering, not the basic protocol.

questions.prompt: The write-ahead logging (WAL) rule requires that:

options.text: The log record for a change reaches stable storage before the modified data page does
Data pages are flushed before their log records
The log is written only at commit time
Undo and redo information are stored in separate files

questions.explanation: WAL guarantees the log always describes any change that might have reached disk, so recovery can undo it. Flushing data first would leave uncorrectable changes after a crash.

questions.prompt: After a crash, ARIES recovery proceeds in which order?
questions.explanation: Analysis rebuilds the dirty page and transaction tables from the last checkpoint; Redo replays history to restore the pre-crash state; Undo then rolls back the losers. Redo-before-undo is what makes repeating history work.

questions.prompt: In deferred database modification, when are a transaction's writes applied to the database?

options.text: During the undo phase of recovery

questions.explanation: Deferred modification buffers updates and applies them post-commit, so recovery needs redo only — an aborted transaction touched nothing. Immediate modification requires both undo and redo.

questions.prompt: What is the primary purpose of a checkpoint in a recovery system?

options.text: To detect deadlocks among running transactions
To release all locks held by active transactions
To bound how much of the log must be examined after a crash

questions.explanation: A checkpoint records a known-good point with buffers flushed, so recovery need not scan the log from the beginning of time. It limits recovery work, not concurrency.

questions.prompt: In multiple-granularity locking, before acquiring an exclusive lock on a row, a transaction must first acquire which lock on the table?
questions.explanation: Intention locks announce intent down the hierarchy, so a transaction wanting a table-level lock can detect conflicts without inspecting every row. X on a row requires IX (or SIX) on its ancestors.

questions.prompt: Optimistic concurrency control is most appropriate when:

options.text: Transactions are long and highly contended

questions.explanation: OCC skips locking and validates at commit, which is cheap when conflicts are unlikely. Under heavy contention the repeated validation failures and restarts make it perform worse than locking.
